member of the commission. − madam president, mr freitas’ report deals with a proposal that opens the way to the introduction of the principle of environmental impact assessments in the fisheries field. i cannot overstate how important this is in terms of a regime shift and an alignment of fisheries regulation with many other maritime activities. in addition, this principle responds to a very specific objective – that of preventing damage to vulnerable marine ecosystems. the proposal fully embodies the ecosystem approach, which the commission is committed to implementing under the common fisheries policy. through this proposal, we respond to the calls made in 2006 by the united nations general assembly to take effective action to prevent vulnerable marine ecosystems in the high seas from being destroyed or significantly damaged by bottom fishing activities. in relation to vessels that operate in areas for which no international conservation and management regime is in place, it is up to the flag state to regulate the activities of its vessels to ensure this protection. since the european union exerts the regulatory competence of the flag state under international law, we must adopt appropriate measures to respond to this un call by the end of this year. the regulation, as proposed, will thus apply to eu flagged vessels operating in non-rfmo areas of the high seas. we currently have a sizeable fleet operating in the south west atlantic, which is one such area. the text has been designed to established result obligations by flag member states, namely to ensure that no fishing permits are to be given to fish with bottom gears unless an assessment of potential impacts clearly demonstrates low risk for vulnerable marine ecosystems. what this means is that the commission does not go into the detail as to how member states are to conduct such assessments, but rather we fix the minimum standards relating to scientific information and then leave it up to member states to see how to achieve the required results. our proposal stipulates that bottom gears cannot be deployed below a depth of 1 000 metres. the argument that the proposed rule has no scientific basis cannot be sustained. on the one hand, we are still developing our knowledge of the deep oceans and face so much uncertainty that the full application of the precautionary approach is warranted. the proposed depth limit is a reasonable choice, as it does not impinge on current eu fleet activities, which are much shallower. on the other hand, this rule seeks to ensure that we give ourselves time to test how this new regulatory approach works before we allow our fishers to expand into deeper waters. this is about keeping the present state of our activities in place until we know enough to be more confident about expanding them safely. the commission is ready to come back to this specific point in two years’ time, when we submit a report to the council and to this assembly on the regulation’s implementation and effectiveness. it is for these reasons that the commission cannot accept the deletion of this rule as proposed in the report. secondly, mr freitas’ report proposes to amend the provision whereby the regulation would impose full observer coverage in the fleets, and stipulate instead a sampling system. the commission also has difficulty in accepting this amendment since, with the absence of observers, only vms remains as a control tool for monitoring compliance by each vessel with its approved fishing plans. this is not enough, and it is probably unrealistic to expect national fisheries monitoring centres to ensure real-time, individual monitoring of each unit in the fleet. in addition, without an observer on board, the very important ‘move away rule’ in case the vessel accidentally encounters an uncharted ecosystem will simply be inoperative as it is impossible to monitor compliance with this rule by vms. as in the previous case, this requirement can be reviewed in two years’ time to assess its effectiveness. most of the remaining proposed amendments are acceptable to the commission, and many have indeed already been brought forward on similar lines during the council discussions. i would like to thank parliament for the support it has expressed to the commission in our efforts to provide an effective response on this issue.
the rapporteur. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by congratulating the commission on the initiative it has taken in this proposal, firstly, and of course, for two reasons. firstly, because it is in line with and follows up on the initiative and proactivity of the european union in the united nations general assembly on this matter and, secondly, because it is based on a very important principle, namely the impact of the evaluation of fisheries even before authorization to operate is granted. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fisheries sector is not affected by the current crisis. the fact is that in coastal areas it is up to the states to take measures to protect vulnerable ecosystems from bottom fishing. in international waters, the protection of the marine environment is the general responsibility of regional marine conventions, where they exist, while the adoption of measures for the conservation and management of living marine resources and the regulation of the impact of fishing on vulnerable ecosystems is the responsibility of regional fisheries management organisations. however, areas of the high seas remain without any body to regulate fishing practices, which is an invitation to destructive fishing. it is on the basis of this reality that the united nations general assembly, and with the european union also taking the lead, has naturally come to the notion that something must be done to protect these seabeds where there is no control whatsoever. this is a positive action, which should be emphasized, which should be welcomed, as is the commission's own proposal, but it is also a good proposal, we can call it a good one, because we are going to oblige vessels flying the flags of our member states to follow a set of rules which we must ensure that, in parallel, through diplomatic channels, other third countries fishing in the areas we are talking about - deep-sea areas - also follow us, because it is useless for the european union to take the lead and oblige its vessels to carry out these studies, to comply with a set of requirements, if other vessels flying other flags are then going to engage in destructive fishing in the exact area we want to protect. so there is one area where this kind and welcome proposal from the commission must have a consequence in terms of diplomatic efforts and also on the basis of the agreement we have had with the united nations general assembly to be able to take a step forward in this. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fisheries sector is not left behind, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report. i think that this study covers the whole depth from 800 to 1 100 or 1 500 metres, and therefore there will be no need to define clearly the 1 000 metres, which is already protected in another way. however, we are still waiting for some further justification, perhaps technical, which the experts we have heard have not been able to put forward, but i think that the statement of the commissioner so far is not sufficient justification for us to assume that the proposal for 1,000 metres would be valid. however, we are waiting and hoping that the european parliament's proposal can indeed be taken into account following tomorrow's vote.
on behalf of the pse group. madam president, i should like to begin by congratulating our rapporteur on this excellent report and to remind him that what is at stake here is the protection of the seabed, including deep coral reefs, seamounts, hydrothermal vents and deep-sea sponges, which are precious relics of our ecosystems. i would also like to point out that the protection of these ecosystems in the autonomous region of the azores has been in place for a long time and was only called into question by the european institutions in 2003, when they decided to open up fishing in this region indiscriminately without taking into account the need to protect these ecosystems. above all, what i think is most important is that we have fully coherent legislation and the problem of the thousand metres is that it is meaningless to say that you cannot fish beyond the thousand metres outside european waters and that you can fish beyond the thousand metres within european waters - it is meaningless from the point of view of the environmental coherence of the legislation. above all, what also worries me most is that this un resolution - the fundamental resolution 61/105 of 8 december 2006 - concerns several other measures, in particular those relating to the protection of wild turtles that exist on the surface and that, unfortunately, the european commission, instead of implementing this decision in its entirety, has decided to start, therefore, point by point, sector by sector, several years later. this does not seem to me to be the best of legislative techniques; it is better that the whole united nations decision be transposed to the community level and that, both within and outside community waters, this would simplify matters immensely and make the legislation much more operational.
on behalf of the gue/ngl group, in general, in line with the proposals in the report aimed at protecting vulnerable marine ecosystems in the high seas, we stress the need for measures to be taken in this context to be based on scientific research in fisheries and to be appropriate, particularly in the light of the diversity of existing situations. the report also stresses the need to find a definition based on the best available scientific information. in the same vein, there is a need to distinguish between the different consequences of the use of different gears, assessing through scientific research on fisheries their potential impacts on resources and the seabed. finally, we reiterate that we still consider it to be the responsibility of each member state to decide on the scope of questions relating to inspections or omissions of observation.
member of the commission. − madam president, i welcome the number of points and comments that have been made, which underline the importance you attach to the issue of dealing with destructive fishing practices. as i said earlier, our proposal responds to a call by the international community and we must show our determination to meet that call. on the issue of the proposed 1 000-metre depth limit, i wish to say that it is crucial that we adopt a precautionary approach, and this chosen limit was designed in a way that provides us with an assurance that we do not have a sudden development of fisheries in a particular area. at the same time, it does not, at this juncture, actually affect current fisheries, and if this is the case i do not understand why there is such resistance to the 1 000-metre limit. but i will look into it again and i am hopeful that this issue can be resolved satisfactorily in the council in june. however, i would also say that i do not agree that we should allow unlimited bottom fishing until we have identified vulnerable ecosystems, because once the harm is done, it is done, and then it is too late. this is why we insist on the precautionary approach. on the issue of observers, let me say that this is a crucial point if we are to show that we are serious about the protection of vulnerable marine ecosystems in the high seas. having full coverage is a key point for the commission. i am confident that we can find a solution to this issue too in the council in june without abandoning the principle of full observer coverage.
the rapporteur. - i regret that the commissioner has not paid attention to what almost all of us members have said, and what the report itself says about the 1000 metres. there is no, and i repeat, there is no scientific evidence that the thousand meters number is the right one. why a thousand? why not 800 or 1,200? there's no scientific evidence, and we've had an audience with experts, and we've had the opportunity to have the head of the azores' department of oceanography and fisheries who's done many good, internationally recognized studies of the seabed, and other people i've talked to, other technicians: there's no evidence that 1,000 meters is reasonable. the thousand metres may have been copied from the mediterranean, but we are not talking about the same area, we are talking about completely different areas! and let's see, my friends: i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. if we are asking the fleets to produce scientific studies to determine whether or not there are any vulnerable seabeds, we are being unreasonable. let's not talk then, in a thousand meters. if there are vulnerable deep-sea ecosystems, they may be at 800 or 1200, but the studies that we force the fleets to submit for fishing licenses will show it: it's as simple as that, and so i think it's a matter of reasonableness in relation to this question. in conclusion, just one last reference to the importance of this subject: it is often said that we know the lunar surface better than the deep sea floor, and so here we are, obliging us, the private sector, to help us to know the deep sea floor better.

in writing. − iuu fishing is one of the biggest problems facing the management of marine resources today. it is a threat to the sustainability of resources and marine biodiversity and has serious economic consequences for fishermen who are legally fishing. the european community, as a major consumer and importer of fishery products, has a particular responsibility in combating illegal fishing and in adopting solutions to prevent the continuation of such practices, as well as in putting pressure on the international community to adopt similar measures. the european parliament's report contains 65 amendments which complement the commission's proposal and are contrary to national interests. the proposal sets out a system applicable to all iuu fishing activities or associated activities carried out on community territory or in waters under the sovereignty or jurisdiction of member states, which was widely discussed and advocated during the portuguese eu presidency. this document therefore deserves my vote in favour.
in writing. − the sustainability of fisheries resources is essential to ensure the long-term viability of fishing and the socioeconomic viability of the fisheries sector. illegal, unreported and unregulated (iuu) fishing threatens this sustainability and jeopardises the viability of the sector and the fishing communities that depend on it. as such, it is essential that measures are taken to strengthen the fight against these illegal activities, in particular by strengthening the control mechanisms in each member state. this proposal, which complements measures already provided for under the common fisheries policy, introduces a number of provisions aimed at curbing such practices by both vessels flying the flag of a member state and those of third countries. the commission is proposing, among other things, greater controls by member states in their ports, the requirement for a certificate from the flag state that the fish is legal and the creation of a list of vessels involved in iuu fishing. however, we reiterate that future consistency between these proposals and a future revision of community control standards should safeguard the competences of the member states, particularly with regard to inspections. we also reaffirm that the whole range of sanctions is a matter for the member states.
in writing. − by their nature, some marine ecosystems (such as reefs, seamounts, hydrothermal vents, coldwater corals or coldwater sponge beds) are vulnerable to the use of certain fishing gear. this proposal aims to protect these ecosystems on the high seas, in particular in areas not regulated by a regional fisheries management organisation. we agree in substance with the proposal submitted and the report voted, but we reiterate that certain aspects of the proposal deserve better clarification. for example, as regards the definition of 'vulnerable marine ecosystem', the report stresses the need to find a definition, in particular within the fao and in accordance with the 'best scientific information', given the lack of in-depth scientific knowledge about these ecosystems. or, as we have said, there is also the need to distinguish the consequences of using different gear, assessing through scientific research on fisheries their potential impacts on resources and the seabed. finally, it is not too much to say that we consider that the scope of issues relating to inspections or observation missions on fishing vessels is a matter for each member state, particularly when new levels of federal deepening are announced under the common fisheries policy.

in writing. - many of the guidelines set out in the report are correct, to which we contribute with some amendments, in particular those relating to the 'increasing difficulties' faced by young farmers, the high costs of setting up and the level of indebtedness and the lack of available holdings. we have put forward a number of proposals which we will bring to the attention of the european commission in the future, including: - the need to take the necessary measures to support, accompany and advise young farmers on their first installation, with a view to increasing success rates and, at the same time, minimising or eliminating situations of withdrawal or even bankruptcy; - the creation of a land bank to be set up on the basis of the land released by early retirement; - the need to establish support for the joint acquisition of high-cost machinery and equipment with low individual use. however, we consider the measures adopted insufficient in the face of the existing problems and which make portugal the member state of the european union with the lowest percentage of young farmers (less than 4%). the cap must be revised in such a way that the value of production is properly assessed and fair prices are set for production.
in writing. − in recent decades, european rural areas have been becoming more desertified, a trend which has been accompanied by a progressive ageing of the population. this ageing of the agricultural population is worrying for the future of european agriculture, and i therefore find the veraldi report very relevant in considering the various aspects relating to the expectations and opportunities for young farmers - who have a key role in the sustainable development of european rural areas. i consider young farmers to be of particular importance for the development of a dynamic agricultural industry in pursuit of the objectives of the lisbon strategy. in the new cap, therefore, the transition between generations must be one of the priorities.

in writing. - while not ignoring some of the positive aspects of the report voted on today, concerning the provision of information or the facilitation of certain banking procedures for consumers, it does not fail to place access to these services within the framework of a liberalised financial market, the aim of which, by its nature, is the pursuit of higher profits and not consumer protection. that is why we abstained. it is not enough to ensure the right to a bank account. we must ensure that no fees or other penalties are charged to customers for any and all services, particularly and most severely hitting the financially weak, those with accounts with lower balances and movements, or simply because they hold bank accounts. it is essential to ensure the public service that also exists in the financial sector, without which we will have worsening social inequalities, dramatically affecting people with fewer financial resources, social solidarity institutions and other social organisations, including micro and small enterprises.
in writing. − the liberalisation of retail financial services in the single market is the latest proposal from the european commission following the liberalisations envisaged in the lisbon strategy, thus attempting to take a further step towards the full liberalisation of services in the european union. in this way, and following other initiatives, it proposes the liberalisation of different retail financial services, including banking, insurance and pension products, in an attempt to remove what it considers to be remaining obstacles, using the old arguments of lower prices and greater choice for consumers, when experience itself shows exactly the opposite. it is the big companies that progressively increase their profits at the expense of more expensive services charged to consumers. even if we welcome the approval of the amendment proposed by our group in defence of the marketing of savings and old age pension products, which should be treated with particular caution, since consumer decisions in this area are generally of great importance and are normally taken only once in a lifetime, the truth is that the majority of the report is negative. that is why we are voting against it.

in writing. − this regulation aims to ensure a high level of protection against counterfeiting and falsification of the euro by defining the measures necessary for its protection by means of checks on banknotes and coins to verify their authenticity and fitness for circulation. according to the latest statistics, in 2007, some 561 000 counterfeit notes and 211 100 counterfeit coins were withdrawn from circulation. the european central bank and the commission respectively having established the definitive procedures to be used for detecting counterfeit notes and coins, it became essential to amend the 2001 regulation, as the institutions involved in the supply of currency to the public now had the tools they needed to carry out this control. i also welcome the express obligation on credit institutions and other relevant institutions to check the authenticity of the banknotes and coins they receive before putting them back into circulation. at the same time, they should make the necessary adjustments to their internal procedures and modernise their equipment. it is also important that the authenticity of the euro is guaranteed in member states which are not part of the euro area but where it circulates as a currency of transaction, although the control methods cannot be applied in the same way and specific verification procedures should therefore be established.

in writing. − an area with shared external borders and internal borders removed has to harmonise some rules on the entry, movement, stay and exit of third country nationals. a prosperous economy and a welfare state with high levels of protection - even compared with neighbouring countries - must establish rules and conditions for the entry of third country nationals. it is therefore important to regulate and to achieve some consistency between the rules of the different areas of the common border. and to do so with the understanding that immigration is a good, an asset to the countries that receive it and a potential asset to the countries of origin, provided it is regulated and legal. and also knowing that humanity in welcoming people in need will be a sign of civilization that we cannot abdicate. the main points of this report deserve my vote in favour, not least because, by not forcing us to reduce our guarantees, it imposes them, even if insufficiently, where they are absent. finally, understanding the debate that has been going on, i think there is one element that has been overlooked. the fate of immigration, especially intra-european immigration, is changing. given that migration flows are one of the most revealing economic indicators, this data deserved more attention.

in writing. − this is another piece of the third package of measures to liberalise the eu's energy markets, following the recommendations adopted by the european parliament in june 2007. the rapporteur therefore agrees with the granting of wider and more independent powers to regulators, with increased transparency requirements in the market, with the improvement of the framework for cooperation at european level between national regulators and between transmission system operators, with the emphasis on further developing interconnection capacity between member states and with the proposal for ownership unbundling as the most effective, although not the only, means of encouraging investment and avoiding discrimination against new entrants. in other words, the european union has forced the privatisation of a sector which is strategic for economic development and now wants some intervention to avoid the serious problems created by the economic groups which have taken over the sector. the rapporteur himself therefore raises some doubts about the voluntary nature of the application of the codes and rules, arguing that they are mandatory. they just never admit that the solution was to maintain a strong public sector in the energy sector. that is why we are voting against it.
in writing. - this is another element of this energy package. the creation of the agency for the cooperation of energy regulators is part of a global strategy, defined by the european commission and the council, to liberalize and regulate the energy sector, which they have designated as the energy package. the strategy is always the same. first, they privatize the public sector. then problems arise and regulators are created, new bureaucracies, greater control by the big powers over what happens in each member state. the report also calls for the commission to be given the power to adopt and implement the measures necessary to ensure that the eu's financial interests are protected. the imposition of standards, codes, market rules or even decisions at higher levels, serving the interests of economic groups, is a recurring argument, since the agency is a supranational institution with powers in a strategic area - such as energy - that affects horizontally all sectors of society. the consequences of interference in the political strategy and economy of each member state can be serious. it is in this context that we oppose the report.
in writing. − road safety is a priority of european transport policy, a real concern for policy-makers and a pillar for all of us as citizens in the fight against the tragedies that unfortunately happen all too often on european roads. the aim of mr ferrari's report is to strengthen community safety requirements and thus improve the safety of pedestrians. we cannot therefore hesitate to demand the utmost attention and the best instruments at our disposal to ensure safety on our roads. in particular, it is essential that legislative work continues to be carried out with the utmost rigour and that the measures adopted are duly monitored and evaluated in order to ensure that the necessary improvements are introduced in a timely and preventive manner. we recognize in this report the attempt to state ways of making up for the backlog and to assert that the proposed prevention systems are the most correct and the most convenient for the victims of motor vehicle collisions. finally, and because the devil sometimes lurks in the details, our task is to ensure, even in the most technical areas, that the legislation we produce always offers the best means of protecting our citizens.
in writing. - this report deals with some positive changes in the usual procedure between the european commission and the european parliament. accordingly, article 5a of decision 1999/468/ec, as amended, introduced the new regulatory procedure with scrutiny for measures of general scope designed to amend non-essential elements of a basic act adopted in accordance with article 251 of the treaty, inter alia, by deleting some of those elements or by supplementing the basic act by the addition of new non-essential elements. following an examination of the existing legislation and these procedures, the commission has put forward this proposal, which covers 59 legislative acts to be adapted to the new regulatory procedure with scrutiny. in its decision of 12 december 2007, the conference of presidents designated the committee on legal affairs as the committee responsible for this alignment of the comitology and the specialised committees as the committees responsible for delivering opinions. the conference of committee chairs reached agreement on 15 january 2008 on the modalities of cooperation between the legal affairs committee and the other committees. the report therefore contains a limited number of amendments which were suggested by other committees in their opinions, which were received in the form of letters.

the subject we are discussing has to do with road safety. however, this proposal for a directive has already suffered a number of accidents along the way. the committee on transport initially rejected the commission's proposal as superfluous and not in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity. after the council had agreed on a general approach to de-bind the annexes to the directive and restrict their application to the transeuropean road networks, it was finally possible - thanks to the efforts of the rapporteur, whom i would like to congratulate - to adopt a report in the committee on transport. the report not only relieves the text of bureaucratic constraints, but also takes into account the different levels of road safety management in different countries. the report also gives priority to the concept of exchanging good practice, always seeking better coordination of action by the union and the member states. it is therefore with satisfaction that we are debating the subject again, this time in the face of a text which offers renewed added value, which reflects the capacity to generate synergies in union action and which points us towards more appropriate solutions where the reality, as we know, is quite different. this is a clear signal to the citizens that, despite the accidents on the way, we are not stranded. in this context, it is proposed to define guidelines and best practices for all stages of road management, from road safety impact assessments to audits, network safety management and inspections. it should be stressed that the directive, as amended, will not require the adoption of technical standards or procedures. it encourages member states, through guidelines, to make the best use of the defined methodologies, even inviting them to apply them to national highways not included in the tens. mr. president, in closing, i would like to say... in 2001, the european union set an ambitious target of halving the number of deaths on european roads by 2010. we hope that this directive, together with many other initiatives already discussed and adopted here, will also help to save many lives of road users crossing the european road network.

on behalf of the pse group. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, first of all, on behalf of the socialist group, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on her work, on her efforts to reach consensus with the shadow rapporteurs and on the efforts made to reach the desirable agreement between the parties. the proposal for a regulation on flavourings aims to clarify and update the rules on the use of flavourings and food ingredients with flavouring properties, taking into account technological and scientific progress in the field of flavourings, developments in food law in the european union and, at the same time, the requirements for the protection of human health. the regulation lays down general conditions for the use of flavourings or food ingredients with flavouring properties, including a clear definition of flavour, general rules for their use, labelling standards and maximum levels of substances that constitute a risk to human health. the compromise reached in this second reading process is the result of joint work between the commission, the council and parliament. several meetings were held, the most controversial points were negotiated, concessions were made on all sides. the agreement, however, reflects the principles of several amendments proposed by parliament which take into account two fundamental objectives: consumer information and the protection of consumers' interests, as well as the protection of public health. flavourings and flavouring substances must be safe and their use must not mislead the consumer. in this context, the new legislation sets maximum levels for the presence of certain substances in flavourings and food ingredients with flavouring properties that are potentially toxic and risky to human health, taking into account the scientific advice of the european food safety authority. these maximum levels do not apply to three substances: estragol, saffrol and methyl eugenol, provided that they are present in compound foods to which no flavouring has been added and only food ingredients with flavouring properties in the form of herbs and/or spices have been added. however, this exception should be reviewed if scientific evidence emerges that their consumption poses health risks. the concept of natural is still confusing to consumers, but the new proposal on the labelling of natural flavourings is more effective in meeting consumer expectations, with the use of the term 'natural' restricted to flavourings obtained from natural flavouring substances where at least 95% of the flavouring compound should be obtained from the natural source to which it refers.
mr president, parliament must give a democratic interpretation of democracy. this means that the rules of procedure are not an aseptic dictate, they must be read in the light of the moral foundation of suffrage and the principle of representation, while signifying self-legislation, the autonomy of the citizens. i would like to take a few notes on this principle. the amendment proposed by mr corbett is, in my view, in principle correct, but the reason why a group which no longer has the minimum number of members required during a parliamentary term should be retained is mainly because the democratic choice of the electors is also almost always made taking into account the position of the candidates in the european parliament's groups. it is not indifferent to the voters whether a candidate is elected to sit on the pse benches or to sit on the ppe benches. i think that this amendment should contain, instead of a discretionary power of the president of parliament, a binding power, instead of a permission, a duty, and the deadline for the continuation of the group can only, from the point of view of democracy, be precisely the deadline of a legislature. otherwise we completely subvert the principles of freedom that constitute us. the second point concerns the temptation to copy the models of the national parliaments. the models of the national parliaments are indeed models for us, but in this case we must copy them cum grano salis, with caution, because the pulverization of groups can, in european democracy, compensate for the deficit of representativeness that throws europe from crisis to crisis. the spraying here can be a compensation for the persistent divorce between european citizens and their representatives. the more plurality there is, the more intense the political struggle and game that normally leads to our consensus will be, because systematic consensus is not without controversy here either. the plurality of groups can help parliament to politicise bureaucratic europe, because a democracy is a democracy, not an order.

in writing. − the report is intended to follow up the 2003 protocol on strategic environmental assessment to the 1991 unece espoo convention on environmental impact assessment in a cross-border context (eia protocol). the commission signed the epa protocol on behalf of the european community on 21 may 2003 at the fifth ministerial conference on the environment for europe, held in kiev, ukraine in may 2003. the objective of the epa protocol is to provide a high level of protection of the environment, including health, and to ensure the integration of environmental and health concerns into measures and instruments to promote such sustainable development. in this context, the european community intends to implement article 13 of the protocol on strategic environmental assessment in the espoo convention through the impact assessment processes set out in the impact assessment communications, which address in a balanced way the economic, social and environmental components of sustainable development.
in writing. − with the signing in october 2004 of the agreement on the accession of switzerland to the schengen acquis, it was not possible to associate liechtenstein due to the lack of an agreement on the taxation of savings (which was not concluded until a year later). given that a policy of free movement of persons between switzerland and liechtenstein has existed for several decades, it was essential to associate liechtenstein to that agreement. i therefore support this initiative, which, by means of a protocol annexed to the agreement, associates this country with schengen, which should accept and apply the entire acquis, with the exception of any provisions of a new act or measure concerning the execution of search warrants and/or the seizure of evidence in the context of investigations or proceedings for offences in the field of direct taxation (which are not punishable by deprivation of liberty under its national law). i support the rapporteur's position - ewa klamt's - that the ep should give a favourable opinion, as it did for the agreement to which this protocol is linked. it is essential, however, that the ep has access to more information on any international negotiations in progress, so that it can exercise its powers in a consistent and effective manner.
in writing. − the current regulation established a standard model visa, but did not ensure a single numbering of visas in the member states. the number is entered to identify the individual visa issued to a third-country national by one of the member states and, although there were some differences between member states, these were not relevant as the visa was only checked at the border, either visually or by optical reading. however, once the visa information system (vis) becomes operational, the external border controls should focus on the visa sticker number in combination with the fingerprints of the holder. it is therefore necessary to change the numbering of visas so that there is a single visa sticker number that can ensure that during the verification process only the relevant application file is called, in relation to which the fingerprints of the person presenting himself at the border will be verified. i therefore support this proposal to ensure a consistent and unique numbering of the visa stickers to be used in the vis, ensuring that when this visa data exchange system comes into force it can function in the most correct way, reducing the risks of improper access to personal data.
in writing. - this is a contradictory proposal, which is why we abstained. while there are some aspects which may be positive, in particular the one concerning a possible amendment to the statute of the court of justice, in order to guarantee the european parliament the right to submit its own observations to the court whenever its prerogatives are directly or indirectly called into question, so that the intervention of the european parliament, when it is not officially a party to the case, is not subject to the discretion of the court of justice, the truth is that others may simply mean a reinforcement of federalism. and in that case, we disagree. we also consider it essential that the european parliament should respect the sovereignty of the member states and therefore also of the national courts. we do, however, accept that a policy of cooperation between the european parliament and the national courts may be of interest. but we insist that it is not acceptable that such cooperation should be used to undermine national rights, including the sovereignty of national courts, and the principle of subsidiarity.
in writing. - there is a need to make the approval process for food additives more transparent and to strengthen consumer protection, particularly for those who are intolerant to certain substances. similarly, environmental protection should be one of the several factors to be taken into account when approving the use of an additive. as already approved at first reading, the consequences of misleading the consumer must be clarified and environmental protection included among the factors to be taken into account when approving the use of an additive. the amendments now adopted at second reading are essentially aimed at improving these aspects to be taken into account in the final text, with a view to strengthening consumer and environmental protection and clarifying the conditions for the approval of additives. from the entry into force of this regulation, food additives will have to meet these requirements.
in writing. - in this report we have attached particular importance to those aspects which claim to seek to safeguard food safety, taking into account the interests of consumers, among which is most notably the desire to purchase food as natural as possible. it is well known that not all toxicologically safe flavourings are beneficial to consumers. this is why we must guarantee the right of choice for consumers. in the context of the flavour approval process, 'reasonable technological needs' are linked to other eu strategies, notably the fight against obesity, as the addition of excessively strong flavourings can serve to hide the poor quality of prepared foods. the council and the european parliament have a different approach to the issue of certain food ingredients with flavouring properties for use in and on foods and the maximum levels of these ingredients set out in annex iii. we know that the principle that herb and spice producers must refute the legal presumption of harmfulness of each product separately is questionable. it would be more logical to reverse the procedure. it's a subject that's going to continue to be controversial.
in writing. - this report refers to a regulation which aims to establish standards and procedures for the authorization of food enzymes, except those which are considered food additives. the european commission notes that the industry has been pushing for harmonisation of legislation establishing a common authorisation procedure for food enzymes, as the absence of community standards in this area has given rise to unfair commercial practices. the european parliament insists on including several important amendments which it adopted at first reading of the commission's proposal for a regulation. it therefore reaffirmed its view that the precautionary principle should be at the heart of any risk assessment and should be emphasised in the proposal. it also strengthened consumer protection provisions to ensure that the use of a food enzyme does not mislead the consumer as to the nature, quality or content of a product, and this concept has been reintroduced. on the other hand, food enzymes are not, and cannot be, genetically modified microorganisms. it is also necessary to avoid that they are derived from gmos. but if it ever happens, it should be clearly identified so as not to mislead consumers. it is essential to ensure a high level of food safety.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the recommendation for second reading of the peter liese report on the inclusion of aviation in the greenhouse gas emission allowance trading scheme, because i consider it essential and urgent to limit the global temperature increase to +2°c. the aviation sector is booming - carbon dioxide emissions from aviation have increased by 87% since 1990 and are expected to double by 2020 - and measures are needed to send a clear signal internationally of the eu's commitment to combating climate change, with a view to achieving an international agreement before the copenhagen conference in 2009. the compromise also includes very positive aspects, such as the derogation scheme for the outermost regions, the use of proceeds from the auctioning of emission allowances to combat climate change and measures to combat deforestation.
in writing. - the proposal voted on in the european parliament is already a compromise, albeit an unsatisfactory one, compared with the european commission's initial proposal, which did not take account of the problems of countries in economic difficulties, in particular the outermost regions. we know that pollution must be reduced, but we must take account of the difficulties of the countries with the weakest economies. the compromise now voted does not avoid all the negative consequences of this trade, but minimises several, postponing the date of entry into force of the first ep proposal, reducing the scope of the auctions and the pressure on the weakest companies. the negotiation of an exception for the outermost regions has become a very important issue here, since the original proposal of the european commission did not, as is well known, provide for any exception for these regions, which meant that all flights originating in or destined for these regions would be covered by the general scheme. in the text finally agreed, the possibility of an exception was preserved, but its scope is not as wide as it should be. we therefore insist on the abolition of this system of trading licences not only for flights between islands but also between islands and the continent.
in writing. - we voted against this report because it is part of a central objective of atrophying the democratic and pluralist functioning of the european parliament. the majority, on the basis of a principle which is not even true - the existence of the renewal treaty - is in fact seeking to reduce the rights and to hinder the members' capacity for initiative, to increase the power of the president of the european parliament and, as a consequence, to impoverish the pluralism of parliamentary debate. this question of democratic impoverishment and the capacity of members to intervene is also clear in the establishment of guidelines on the procedure for written questions to the council and the commission. however, this decision is only one part of the more general anti-democratic line which the majority of the european parliament is following, in particular its largest political groups (epp and pse), of which another essential part is the demand for new, more restrictive criteria for the formation of political groups, which also deserves our denunciation and strong protest.

mr president, the most important issue being discussed here is the liberalisation of the natural gas market, putting pressure on the member states to speed up the process of privatisation of what is still public. to achieve this more quickly, they insist on the separation of ownership from the grids, without concern for energy security itself. the fact is that the results of the liberalization of the electricity market show that neither workers nor consumers have benefited from it. on the contrary, it has reduced entitlement employment and increased the prices paid by consumers. of course, the profits of the economic groups in the electricity sector have increased, but so-called energy poverty has increased, meaning that more people and households have difficulty accessing energy. so we regret that they are going down the same path as natural gas. although these are different sectors, the economic and social consequences will be the same. hence our opposition.
on behalf of the pse group. other opening up to trade and investment is a cornerstone of the construction of europe. sovereign wealth funds are an old reality. in the present context of serious financial imbalances, as has been said, its collection and the interest in its collection have increased. the opening up of strategic sectors and the provision of essential public goods to private initiative is another feature of the european union. but it is important to ensure that all operators, and sovereign funds in particular, are governed by clear and transparent rules and that their objectives are compatible with the proper functioning of markets, fair competition between operators and the protection of the rights of european citizens in the short and long term. we welcome the commission's commitment to a multilateral code of conduct under the aegis of the international monetary fund. but, as with hedge funds, as with private equity, a code of good practice is not enough. the commission is called upon to provide an autonomous and much stronger guarantee that the principles of proper transparency and governance are respected by all financial actors in the internal market, including these funds, and with european criteria not just national or international ones.

madam president, commissioner, at a time when the air transport sector is going through one of its most difficult crises as a result of the unstoppable increase in fuel prices, it is essential that we invest our attention and our legislative effort in measures which help to maintain the strength and dynamism of this sector. in this context, the commitment to improving the common rules for operating air services in the community had to cover a number of key points: first, the strengthening of the requirements for the financial capacity of airlines, given the potential link between the financial soundness of carriers and safety; second, transparency in the pricing of tickets, with clear indication, in addition to the basic fare, of taxes, fees and other charges; and, finally, the unequivocal definition of public service obligations, including the conditions arising from the specific constraints of the outermost regions and the need to safeguard competition. the rapporteur has proposed that we vote on the council's common position. this means that, in addition to the points already mentioned, the main objectives identified by parliament at first reading have been achieved. the text does indeed formulate and define correct rules on the issue of operating licences, aircraft leasing, public service obligations and traffic distribution rules, strengthening the internal market and passenger rights. it also gives the commission the right to negotiate intra-community traffic rights with third countries and strengthens the social rights of those working in the sector. i would therefore like to congratulate mr degutis on his work on this dossier and support the adoption of the council's common position without further amendments. the two arms of the legislature worked together and reached a relevant agreement. will the result help to overcome the crisis? i would like to hear the commissioner's answer. and will it contribute to a better and more efficient internal aviation market for the benefit of the economy and citizens? we hope so.

the report by mr karl von wogau, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, on space and security (2008/2030 (ini)) (a6-0250/2008) follows.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, i congratulate mr karl von wogau on this report and on his tireless advocacy of deepening the european project by building a defence europe. the report reflects the appropriate balance between what should be the main objectives of a european space and security policy: firstly, the paramount importance of preventing, by all diplomatic and political means, the placing of weapons in space, as commissioner verheugen has stressed, so that space can continue to be used as the common property of all humanity; secondly, the importance of equipping europe with the special policies, financial resources and equipment needed to ensure its strategic autonomy on the international scene. as regards the first objective, it should be stressed that this is not a question of combating the use of space for military purposes. we know that since the beginning of space exploration, satellites have been used to support the armed forces of various countries, particularly in the field of communications. some of our colleagues are trying to confuse this kind of function, which is compatible with international law, with the recent attempts by some, especially the united states of america, to put weapons in space, thus turning it into the fourth dimension of the battlefield, beyond land, sea and air. it is this bellicose strategy and other unacceptable initiatives, such as china's anti-satellite test in january 2007, that must be fought. the report responds to these threats by calling for a proactive diplomatic role for the european union. it is up to europe to lead a comprehensive strategy to equip the international community with an effective legal architecture to ensure the total exclusion of weapons from space, including through the revision and strengthening of the outer space treaty. the report calls for the crucial importance of space for europe's strategic autonomy to be taken into account. taking the example of the galileo project, an overwhelming majority of members of this parliament believe that sharing financial resources, technology and equipment among europeans is the only way for europe not to be dependent on the united states of america, russia or china for strategically vital activities such as navigation. the report also highlights the often ignored or feared importance of galileo and other european national programmes for a serious common foreign and security policy. without the peaceful and efficient use of space, our economies, our transportation, our weather, our way of life today, would be impossible. it is up to europe to think strategically about this area of strategic importance, as is already being done in washington, beijing and moscow. think and act. and in this context i regret that the presidency of the council is not present in this debate today.

the following is the report by mrs sarah ludford, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council amending the common consular instructions to diplomatic missions and consular posts with regard to the introduction of biometric data, including the provisions on the organisation of the reception and processing of visa applications (com (2006) 0269 - c6-0166/2006 - 2006/0088 (cod)) (a6-0459/2007).
mr president, mr vice-president of the commission, ladies and gentlemen, we wanted this initiative to ensure interoperability between all member states, to ensure the same level of protection of personal data and the fair treatment of all asylum seekers. i particularly support the efforts to make it easier for applicants to apply for visas through the one-stop shop system and the collection of biometric data, i.e. the facial photograph and the 10 fingerprints of visa applicants, which will be stored in the central system, the vis. it should be stressed that this data will be used for identification purposes, as vice-president barrot has already mentioned, which is quite different from the situation in european passports, where only two fingerprints are allowed to be taken, so that they cannot be used for purposes other than verification, i.e. one-to-one comparison. in this respect, i welcome the willingness of the european commission, as now revealed to the house by vice-president barrot, to cooperate in the study requested by parliament on the reliability of fingerprints of minors. now, mr president, since we are in the process of a complete revision of the community visa code, a separate discussion of this particular proposal would only make sense if this process could be speeded up. this objective was not achieved. we shall vote tomorrow on a text which has not been agreed at first reading and which represents only the first stage in a process which is proving to be long. i therefore have serious doubts about the need to continue to discuss this proposal separately when its timetable seems to me to be very similar to that of the revision of the code itself that is being discussed.
the commission's communication and the proposal for a regulation to the council, if there were any doubts, would suffice to confirm that the measures proposed therein are not intended to address the causes which are actually at the root of the current worsening socioeconomic situation in the fisheries sector. despite some measures that meet the just demands of the overwhelming majority of the fishing industry, what is in view is once again the use of the deterioration of the financial situation of this sector to push forward with measures that further encourage and accelerate the culling of vessels. it is stressed that no concrete proposal has been put forward to address the two major issues that arise: the increase in the price of fuels, diesel and petrol, and the formation and improvement of the price of fish at first sale without this increasing in the consumer, that is, there are no financial resources to coordinate and implement measures to help the sector cope with the increase in fuel costs. however, there are many hundreds of millions of euros to promote the slaughter of vessels, that is, market measures are mentioned, but the painful part is not touched upon, namely the fair distribution of added value in the value chain. the commission is basically reaffirming and putting forward a set of proposals which are inadequate in their essence because they do not meet the needs of the overwhelming majority of the fisheries sector, and which show that the only real objective is the destruction of a large part of this strategic economic sector.
mr president, i think that the political direction taken by this proposal and its timeliness are absolutely indisputable. i think that is the kind of measure that is appropriate to the situation we are experiencing in european seas. i think it's about the convenient direction. the great problem that arises, particularly when we look at this proposal with some caution, is its applicability, because the commissioner asked us for urgency, our parliament gave him all the urgency, we waived the right to analyse and propose amendments to the regulation. but the problem is whether rules of such complexity as those before us are feasible within the time limits envisaged. i remember that one of the clauses requires that the slaughter plans must start before 30 november, but at the same time these slaughter plans must have programmes drawn up by the member states, that in some cases these programmes must be approved by the european commission, that the financial means must first come from reprogramming of the european fisheries fund, which is already in force, reprogramming which is extremely complex and with clauses, mandatory percentages, some of which are almost impossible to read, as the commissioner has just had the opportunity to see with article 19 (4). that seems to me to be the big problem - if we do not have in this detail of your proposal the big devil that can make its practical application impossible, which would be absolutely regrettable. i would therefore ask the commission, the commissioner and all the staff of the directorate-general to look at the feasibility of what is proposed here, because if it is not feasible within the timeframe proposed it will not be worth the effort that is being asked of us here.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the fisheries sector is, in the whole of the economy, probably the one that is suffering the most from the current oil shock. we all know that. the commission's political signal with this package of measures is therefore welcome, and it will not be the european parliament that will prevent its rapid adoption, as all the members have mentioned. we know that, given the scale of the problem, there are no magic solutions. however, after examining the commission's proposals, i cannot hide my great disappointment. all the measures point in one direction: the killing of boats. even alleged emergency measures, such as temporary stops, are necessarily linked to fleet reduction commitments. it is not understood that measures under article 7 exclude the replacement of engines, nor is it understood that vessels are eligible under fleet adaptation schemes if their fuel consumption represents more than 30% of production costs. what about the other vessels, commissioner, which are almost all but the trawlers? what about the entire coastal fleet with a huge social weight? i also do not understand why only vessels using only one fishing gear and representing 70% of the fleet using that gear are eligible for partial culling. this requirement, together with the rule of reducing capacity by 60% and the limit of 25% of this capacity for supporting new vessels, makes this measure absolutely unworkable, as my colleague mr casaca said a moment ago. i understand, commissioner, that you have difficulty finding solutions to problems of this magnitude, but we cannot give the sector the illusion that we are giving it a remedy for its problems when it is leading to slaughter and neglect. it is better in this case to say it explicitly. i therefore call on you, despite the short time you have until monday's council, to make an effort to simplify and to be realistic, so that the positive political signal does not turn into a huge disappointment for the sector, which looks to us with great hope.
madam president, i would like to draw attention to the fact that we have just rejected an amendment asking for the release of someone we nominated for the sakharov prize. the next time we award the sakharov prize, in december, we had better give them a set of chains and they can go straight to jail! in writing. − the objectives of this proposal for a regulation are to organise the reception and processing of visa applications with regard to the entry of biometric data into the visa information system (vis) at eu level, providing, firstly, for the obligation to provide biometric data to be stored in this system and the rules for doing so and, secondly, for the provisions on the organisation of the reception of visa applications. the proposal, which is part of the community's border management (schengen area), makes operational the collection of 'biometric identifiers' (photographs and fingerprints) of visa applicants, a measure which is at least questionable, where a number of issues remain to be clarified, in particular as regards: its effectiveness, the protection of these personal data, the objectives and criteria for collection, the rules on the content of vis files, access rights (in particular in the framework of agreements between the eu and different countries on the exchange of information), and finally the safeguarding of citizens' rights, freedoms and guarantees. we are opposed to the communitization of justice and home affairs and the creation of structures and instruments for surveillance and control at eu level, promoting security-oriented policies. that is why we are voting against it.
in writing. - i welcome the maintenance of the fisheries protocol with mauritania, although it is worth noting that the negotiation process for it has not always been conducted in the most open and transparent manner. the member states were not sufficiently consulted during the negotiating period, which resulted in a protocol that considerably reduces fishing opportunities while keeping the financial compensation virtually unchanged. the technical aspects essential for the main fleets have not been resolved, but new limitations have been imposed, including an extraordinary biological rest period without great scientific rigor. despite the above, portugal maintains a reasonable position with regard to its fishing opportunities in these fisheries, namely 886 gt per year for class 1 (crustacean vessels, except for lobster and crab), obtains a licence in category 5 (cephalopods) and maintains 300 gt for lobster. on the basis of the above, i consider this agreement to be a positive one for my country and i shall vote in favour of it.
in writing. - the fisheries sector has been one of the sectors of the economy most affected by the current energy crisis. the skyrocketing fuel prices, the reduction in fishing effort introduced by the cfp and the stagnation in the prices of fish at first sale have put shipowners and fishermen in a delicate position. the proposal for a council regulation is therefore justified as a matter of urgency, since it aims to ensure that the eu fleet is adapted to the current economic situation dictated by the energy crisis. this proposal follows on from a commission communication, which gives a clear picture of the problems and constraints facing fisheries and the measures needed to alleviate the current crisis. although i welcome the initiative which has been taken in presenting this regulation, i think it falls a little short of what would be expected after reading the abovementioned communication. the temporary cessation of fishing activities in article 6, with mandatory integration into fleet restructuring plans, the exclusion of engines in article 7, the whole of article 9 and article 12 (3), which only defends the interests of trawling, seem to me to be the least achieved points in this proposal. despite the above, and given the great difficulties facing the fisheries sector at european level, this document deserves my vote in favour.
in writing. as we said in the debate yesterday, there are good reasons for voting against this proposal for a regulation. if there were any doubts about its correctness, it would have been enough to have followed the interventions of the european commission to dispel them. for the european commission the problem is overcapacity and the objective and solution is 'fleet restructuring'. what socioeconomic crisis? what increase in fuel (diesel and, stressed, petrol)? what's the price of the fish at the first sale? the commission's position is quite simple: 'if there is a greater reduction in capacity by some member states, it will benefit other member states, because if there is a reduction in capacity with the consequent reduction in effort, there will be more resources and more market opportunities...' the commission is proposing to spend some 1.6 billion euros (!!!) on the scrapping of vessels alone. simply put, if the fisheries sector does not die from the disease, it will die from the cure. there is no money to support the sector in dealing with rising production costs and to safeguard wages. however, eur 1 600 million is proposed for the permanent, partial or 'temporary' cessation of activity. following the motto, the portuguese government has budgeted some €8.2 million for the culling of 27 vessels in 2008.

the rapporteur. - madam president, madam minister, mr commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the process of european integration was initially marked by the communityisation of the economic area. but step by step, the method devised by jean monnet and his founders, the community has moved on to other areas with the concern to bring common problems together and to find common solutions to them. a long and difficult journey that is not yet complete, but which must be followed by firm and decisive steps. one of the areas which presents us all with complex and difficult problems in the european union, which has now expanded to 27 member states and is home to some 500 million people, is justice. justice is one of the pillars of democracy and one of the instruments in the service of freedom. democracy and freedom are two of the union's fundamental values. for this reason, and because of the challenges arising from the process of european construction itself and the new problems of modern life, the court of justice is now, in my view, of vital importance and requires special attention from the union's institutional bodies, which have the power to legislate or to issue resolutions and political guidelines on the matter. trial and sentencing in absentia in criminal proceedings, known as in absentia trials, have different procedural solutions which vary widely from one member state to another. the situation is serious in that the different procedural solutions are a permanent obstacle to the enforcement of criminal judgments in one member state that have been handed down in another member state. this situation makes it difficult, or even impossible, to apply the principle of mutual recognition and increases the crime and insecurity in the union. we therefore welcome the legislative initiative of slovenia, france, the czech republic, sweden, slovakia, the united kingdom and germany, received and supported by the council, which aims in particular to establish procedural rules on notifications, second trials or appropriate remedies and judicial representation to make the action of criminal justice quicker and more effective and effective. the principle of mutual recognition applies in particular to the european arrest warrant and to surrender procedures between member states, in the application of the principle of mutual recognition to financial penalties, confiscation orders and sentences in criminal matters imposing penalties and other measures depriving of liberty for the purpose of enforcement of such sentences by the union, and should also include cases of recognition and of suspended sentences, alternative penalties and conditional sentences. the report i am presenting to this house today has been very well received by libe members. several amendments were tabled by myself and other members, and several compromise amendments were obtained, and there was a strong consensus among the members of the pse, ppe, alde, greens/efa and uen groups, so that the vote was only two votes against. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, this report therefore introduces amendments to the proposal for a council framework decision which, in our view, enriches it technically and gives it political robustness, particularly as regards the procedures for notifying the accused and guaranteeing his rights of defence, the possibility for the accused to be represented in his absence and to be represented by a legal representative appointed and paid by the state, and the possibility of a new trial or an appropriate appeal in accordance with national laws being brought by the accused who has already been tried in absentia. finally, i should like to thank and congratulate the political groups for the effort they have made to reach an understanding and a consensus, and i hope and wish that the vote will at least be equivalent to the broad consensus achieved.
the rapporteur. i should like to thank the minister and the commissioner for their words, as well as my colleagues, those who agreed and those who did not, because those who did not agree give me the opportunity here and now to make some clarifications. but before i do, i want to say this: i am particularly pleased today, as a member of parliament, a lawyer and a citizen, to be able to endorse the council's proposal and our amendments, and i hope and wish that the framework decision will be adopted and implemented. because the situation in europe is serious and we must respond without further delay. there are many already convicted defendants who are moving about the union without the courts being able to enforce the sentences handed down in other countries. this is a serious problem for the development of crime and security in europe and it is important that the european institutions have a response. the framework decision promotes above all the principle of mutual recognition and our amendments, the amendments proposed by parliament, must be read in conjunction, whether the solutions proposed for notifications, the solutions proposed for the rules on the representation of the accused, or the solutions proposed for the appeal or appeal proceedings. it is that in any of these solutions, technical solutions, they are articulated and, in our view, the rights of the defence are guaranteed at all times and in all circumstances to the accused. we know, and it must be said, that the perfect is the enemy of the good. in these circumstances, the solution that has been found, in my view, is a solution that we must adopt, which is already an important and big step forward and is another small step. following the old rule, this is how the european union is built, this is how europe is built.

in writing. − the international debate on chemicals and their role in our lives dates back to 1980, first in the international labour organisation and then at the united nations, which adopted the ghs (harmonised system of classification and labelling of chemicals) in december 2002, and revised it in 2005. these decisions have had an impact at community level, with the adoption of several documents. at the moment, it is only the proposal for a regulation on the classification and labelling of substances and mixtures in which the european union intends to apply the international criteria agreed by the united nations economic and social council for the classification and labelling of dangerous substances and mixtures, also known as the general harmonised system (ghs). this system aims to address the protection of human health and the environment, without affecting the movement of substances and mixtures, by establishing criteria for classification and information, including labelling requirements and safety data sheets. this applies to safeguarding the transport of dangerous goods and to preventing the health and safety of consumers, workers and the environment. that is why we are voting in favour of these reports.

member of the commission. − mr president, i certainly intend to press on with determination in the negotiations to complete the doha world trade deal. it is very important indeed and i am grateful to the honourable member for reinforcing that. i did not actually intend to comment on or respond to this debate. the reason i do so is because i feel that, in some of the contributions that have been made, there has been demonstrated not only a bit of a misunderstanding about the provision of services in the 21st century, particularly amongst developing countries, but, beyond that, a false ideological boundary is being put in place through the remarks of some of those who have contributed to this debate between what they call ‘commercial’ and ‘non-commercial’ services. i have to say that spending most of my time as i do in the world and amongst developing countries, this distinction and this ideological boundary that has been described in this debate is increasingly fading without trace. it is not the case, as mrs lucas has suggested, amongst wto members that developing countries increasingly see trade in services as quite different and separate from trade in goods. actually, the exact opposite trend is occurring in the wto and in trade negotiations. increasingly, developing countries are bringing trade in services into these negotiations. i think that it is wrong – and i speak as somebody who is a social democrat of many decades standing who, i think and i hope, has a developed social conscience – to put forward a proposition in the case of services that state provision is good and that private provision is bad. this is not only out-of-date thinking; it is contrary to the interests of developing countries and to the very needs of the poorest members of those countries and those communities who we should be seeking to stand up for with our values as europeans and our principles as europeans. so i hope that we will not follow and not reinforce, if i can respectfully suggest, this extraordinary equation that you can put the needs of poorest people first by denying to developing countries the opportunities to supply not only water and energy and telecoms more efficiently and more cheaply for consumers, but also supply health care and education using investment, technology, management skills and techniques from a variety of international sources on a competitive basis. this most certainly does not mean that these services therefore should go unregulated. i do not support monopolistic behaviour, price-fixing and cartels, but this goes to the very point that the honourable member was making. regulation by national governments in developing countries is, of course, essential in relation to these services, but please let us not create or give support to what i believe is, as i have described, a false ideological boundary between the commercial and the non-commercial. both are equally valid if properly regulated and if properly serving the needs of the people who are desperately in need of more services of this kind, more efficiently provided and more cheaply in many cases.
in july, another attempt to conclude the 'doha round' aimed at taking a step forward in trade liberalisation failed, as the european parliament intends to approve an (own-initiative) report that pushes to the nausea for the liberalisation of trade in services worldwide, either within the wto or through bilateral or multilateral agreements promoted by the eu with third countries. it is a genuine pamphlet aimed at liberalising all services, including public services, which it calls 'public needs and the general interest'. among other examples, it points to greater liberalisation of healthcare, water distribution, education, cultural services, tourism or financial services. the report goes so far as to state that 'the principles of gats do not prohibit privatisation or deregulation' and stipulates that, after the entry into force of the wto agreement, periodic negotiating rounds should be held 'in order to progressively achieve a higher level of liberalisation'. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly use of energy. the great capital in europe could not write better...
